extracted.intended_audience: EU-based SMEs, IP practitioners and companies seeking to protect or exploit IP in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: A country fiche summarising South African IP law: types of IP rights, registration and procedural requirements, patentability standards, filing routes/timelines, maintenance, enforcement and practical tips for foreign applicants and SMEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered vs unregistered IP rights
rubrics_metrics.description: IP rights in South Africa may be either registered or unregistered; registered rights are formally applied for through government channels, while unregistered rights exist from creation of the IP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main IP rights available are trade marks, patents, designs, copyright, plant breeders’ rights and traditional/indigenous knowledge. Trade secrets/confidential information are protected by common law only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and filing channels
rubrics_metrics.description: All applications for registration are filed in English and Registry functions for trade marks, patents and designs are handled online by CIPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official administrative fees are modest; the Registry produces electronic certificates. Foreign applicants must appoint a local agent as a service address for patent, design and trade mark applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to appoint local agent/service address
rubrics_metrics.description: The South African Patents and Trade Marks Office (CIPC) requires all foreign applicants to appoint a local agent as a service address for patent, design and trade mark applications filed in South Africa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the list of members of the South African Institute of Intellectual Property Law (SAIIPL) for potential agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (absolute novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable an invention must have absolute novelty, not be obvious to a person skilled in the art, and be capable of being used or applied in trade, industry or agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent rights are sought to protect methods/processes, devices, new materials, chemical compounds or compositions. Absolute novelty is expressly required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of patents recognised
rubrics_metrics.description: South African law provides for three types of patents: conventional patents, patents of addition and divisional patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent for a main invention and its patents of addition cannot be assigned separately from each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent filing routes and formality types
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent protection can be obtained by national filing (provisional or complete application), Paris Convention (conventional) application, or via a PCT national phase entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete application can be a national or a Paris Convention priority application. Convention applications must be filed within 12 months from the international filing date. A PCT application must be filed within 31 months from the earliest priority date. On request to the Registrar, 1-3-month extensions are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: No substantive examination by Registry
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications in South Africa are not subject to any substantive examination by the Registry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete national patent applications and conventional applications are typically granted between 12–15 months from filing; PCT national phase applications typically granted between 15–20 months from national phase filing. Acceptance can be delayed at applicant’s request (commonly to await examination in another jurisdiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Once registered, a patent is protected in South Africa for 20 years from the national and international filing date, subject to payment of renewal fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent confers rights to exclude others from making, using, disposing of or importing the patented invention in South Africa for the duration of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment recording requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of a patent application or a registered patent must be in writing and recorded in the Register to be valid against third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an assignment is not recorded, it will not be valid against third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent marking recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not a legal requirement, it is recommended that patented products be marked with the South African registered patent number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design registration eligibility and novelty standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Design registrations protect the physical form of articles of manufacture and are divided into aesthetic and functional designs; an aesthetic design must be new and original, a functional design must be new and not commonplace in the relevant art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute novelty is required for both kinds of designs, subject to a 6-month grace period from the 'release date' (date of first disclosure). Both functional and aesthetic design applications may be lodged for the same article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design examination and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications in South Africa are not subject to substantive examination; once registered, protection is 15 years (aesthetic designs) and 10 years (functional designs) from the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain a valid design registration it must be registered annually from the third anniversary of the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design filing limitations (no Hague; priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa is not a party to the Hague Agreement; priority design applications under the Paris Convention are accepted if filed within 6 months of the priority application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs registered in South Africa are not enforceable outside South Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark registration benefits and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration of trade marks is recommended; registration lasts 10 years from the filing date with renewal terms of 10 years (in perpetuity if renewal fees are paid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The registration process typically takes about 18 months for a straightforward application. The Registry issues electronic certificates. Priority trade mark applications under the Paris Convention are accepted if filed within 6 months of the priority application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark types and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Various types of trade marks can be registered including certification marks, collective marks, word marks, devices, and non-traditional marks (sounds, tastes, scents) provided they are capable of graphical representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only national trade mark filings are accepted as valid and subsisting; South Africa is not a member of ARIPO, OAPI, the Madrid Protocol or Agreement; trade marks registered in South Africa are not enforceable outside South Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-use cancellation vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a non-use period of 5 years after which registered trade marks are vulnerable to cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registered trade marks can be assigned and licensed; it is advisable to search the Trade Mark Registry before adopting a mark because Registry records are limited to marks registered or in the process of registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unregistered trade mark protection (passing off)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unregistered trade marks are protected under common law and can be enforced under the delict of unlawful competition (passing off) where misrepresentation results in a reasonable likelihood of confusion among the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no official records of trade marks that are only in use in the market; perform clearance searches on the Register as part of adoption due diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright basics and registration exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright is an automatic exclusive right for original works providing economic and moral rights; copyright generally does not need to be registered in South Africa except for cinematograph films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many works qualify (literary, musical, artistic works, sound recordings, broadcasts, computer programs). Duration varies by material form and is currently no less than 50 years. Assignment must be in writing and signed to be effective. Use of © is recommended though not legally required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant breeders’ rights eligibility and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant breeders’ rights protect new varieties of plants produced by biological processes; to qualify a variety must be new, distinct, uniform and stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration is 25 years for vines and trees and 20 years for other plants from date of granting; rights must be renewed annually. Seeking protection requires specialised knowledge and local advice is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional/indigenous knowledge protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional knowledge is treated as 'indigenous knowledge' and encompasses a wide range of community-developed knowledge forms which may be protected under existing IP laws (trade marks, copyright, performers’ protection, designs) and by the Indigenous Knowledge Act No 6 of 2019.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once recorded or protected under the appropriate IP law, indigenous knowledge may be commercialised by the owning community. Further details on amendments linking indigenous knowledge to IP laws are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indications (GIs) treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa is not a signatory to the Lisbon Agreement, so Lisbon registrations have no effect in South Africa; national laws and 2019 Regulations implement GI protection for agricultural products and establish a GI Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GIs can also be protected under the Trade Mark Act as collective or certification marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement options (civil, criminal, border measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners of IP rights may take civil action, criminal action, and use border measures; customs have authority ex officio and/or at rights holders’ request to prevent clearance of IP-infringing goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Counterfeit Goods Act 1997 specifically protects owners against counterfeiting and enables civil and criminal actions. Alternative tribunals and ADR Regulations (amended 2017) govern domain name disputes (.za).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing considerations and recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Licences of registered South African rights may be recorded in the relevant Register (not mandatory); licensing rights owned outside South Africa to be used in South Africa is permitted subject to regulatory approvals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition law issues may be relevant to licensing; entering into licence agreements requires specialised local knowledge and advice is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain name and online brand protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The most popular domain for South Africa is '.co.za' and domain names can be registered through accredited registrars listed by the .za central registry (ZACR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should advertise and protect trade marks online and consider domain name strategy as part of brand protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: International treaty participation and practical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa is party to major IP treaties (Berne, Paris, PCT, TRIPS, Budapest, UPOV, WIPO Convention, WTO/TRIPS) but has not ratified or is not party to some (Trademark Law Treaty, WCT, WPPT, Madrid system, Hague, Lisbon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effects include acceptance of Paris Convention priorities (within specified periods) and limitations such as inability to use regional filing systems (ARIPO/OAPI) or WIPO filing routes for designs/trade marks that would automatically cover South Africa.
